speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister. Will the Prime Minister table in the house a copy of the judgment, No. 151177, of Mr. Justice Thorson in the Drew case?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF JUDGMENT AND EVIDENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I shall secure a copy. There is certainly no reason why it should not be tabled.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF JUDGMENT AND EVIDENCE
speechtext: May I ask another question arising out of the one I have already asked. Will the Prime Minister also table the transcript of the evidence heard in this particular case?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF JUDGMENT AND EVIDENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the transcript of the evidence is naturally available to anyone who desires to secure it and will pay the necessary fee. I see no reason-this, of course, is always subject to reconsideration -why that evidence should be tabled. If the hon. gentleman, being a learned member of the bar, would simply make the necessary application and pay the proper fee, no doubt he would be able to secure a copy of the proceedings.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF JUDGMENT AND EVIDENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct another question to the Prime Minister. As a result of our examination on this side of the house of the judgment of Mr. Justice Thorson and, in particular, in view of the fact that such further examination of the judgment and the Prime Minister's statements on the matter have not removed our apprehensions in this case, I wish to ask the Prime Minister whether he will provide an
opportunity for a parliamentary examination in order to elicit the facts and clear up contradictions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF JUDGMENT AND EVIDENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not a question of removing contradictions. The committees are set up in respect of matters affecting the privileges of parliament. If the hon. gentleman in the ordinary course desires such an investigation then he will make the necessary charge, and when the charge is made action will be taken in accordance with the principles that at all times have been applicable to parliamentary procedure.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF JUDGMENT AND EVIDENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Transport. Did the minister make a formal submission to treasury board in connection with the valuation of Mr. Clare?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF JUDGMENT AND EVIDENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I said, I believe all the pertinent evidence in this case was dealt with very effectively by the presiding judge. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF JUDGMENT AND EVIDENCE

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: STATEMENT ON REQUEST THAT CANADIAN STUDENTS HAVE PRIORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Beauce asked me a question on June 5, the translation of which is as follows:
In view of the fact that many Canadian students have to quit college-
And so on.
-I wonder whether the right hon. Prime Minister could assure the house that Canadian students will be given priority over the many foreign students who, according to that Canadian Press dispatch from London-
Which he had already quoted.
-are already here or are expected to be here this summer.
The press report in question indicates that some 500 students intend to come forward to Canada and the United States with a view to taking summer employment. A report has just been received from the Canadian immigration office in London establishing that the commonwealth migration council plans for only 70 of these students to come to Canada. In the past there has been a summer exchange of students between Canada and the United Kingdom. The body that is in charge of this matter has been advised that only those students can come forward who are assured of employment in advance. While it is not proposed to do away completely with the exchange of students, it has been pointed out that only those may come who have available summer employment in advance of their arrival here.

Mr. Speaker, as the house will
probably remember there was some difficulty a few weeks ago in connection with the St. John's housing authority. Objection had been raised by the federal government that it had no representation on that authority. The membership consisted of seven persons. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words will be to thank the hon. member for Belle-chasse (Mr. Dorion) for being here today, because I advised him of my intention to answer certain statements he made in the house on second reading of this bill.
Mr. Speaker, I have found the hon. member for Bellechasse quite different from what he had shown himself to be before coming to this house. It seems that the hon. member had been entrusted with the task of answering, on behalf of the Quebec Conservatives, the excellent speech of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). Well, Mr. Speaker, as I shall presently explain, the hon. member for Bellechasse has in no way taken up the challenge issued by the hon. member for Laurier to the Conservative members from the province of Quebec.
To the great surprise of all those who heard him, the hon. member for Bellechasse declared himself in favour of this bill and, together with several of his fellow-members, he voted for the passing of the bill on second reading. Moreover, I am certain-because he told me so-that the hon. member will vote in favour of the bill on third reading.
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I want to recall in this house that, in order to mark time, and probably also to direct the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) to himself, the hon. member of Bellechasse thought it preferable to put aside the bill then under review and to embark upon a lengthy statement on the Plagiaries of Thunder. Hearing the hon. member made me think of a student of rhetoric who wants to show off before his teacher in order to get good marks. Well, Mr. Speaker, I shall leave my friend, the hon. member for Bellechasse to his Plagiaries of Thunder, and put him in the presence of facts so as to prove to the house how often he can change his mind and also change his colour, like a chameleon, according to the place where he happens to be.

During the last election campaign, I noted several statements by the hon. member for Bellechasse which indicated to what extent that man could change his mind. When he wanted to become a member of parliament, he was saying one thing; but now that he wants to become minister, he says quite another thing.
Mr. Speaker, I say to the hon. member for Bellechasse that if, during the last election campaign, he had expressed the same opinions concerning fiscal arrangements which he did the other day in this house, he would never have been elected, no more than he could hope to become minister if he expressed in the house opinions similar to those he did express in Bellechasse.
Alas! Mr. Speaker, the poor taxpayer! (Text):

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Order. I think before the hon. member pursues these election issues further I should remind him and the house that this is the third reading of Bill C-41, which has one clause only, to provide for the continuation of a provision with respect to income tax in federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. On third reading the debate is not on the principle of the bill; the debate is on the bill itself as it is presented to the house for final approval.
That is a very different matter from debate on second reading. What the hon. member is saying would perhaps have been appropriate on second reading; in fact I have no doubt it would have been, but on third reading I feel that hon. members should observe the precedents. I refer hon. members to Beau-chesne's fourth edition, citation 418, which states:
All amendments which may be moved on a second reading of a bill may be moved on the third reading with the restriction that they cannot deal with any matter which is not contained in the bill.
In other words, only what is contained in the bill is before the house on third reading. Supplementing that, May's sixteenth edition at page 421 states that generally no matter ought to be raised in debate on a question which would be irrelevant if moved as an amendment.
I think it has been the practice of this house to confine the debate on third reading strictly to the contents of the bill itself, and I would ask the hon. member to bear that in mind. If anyone disagrees with my interpretation I would be glad to hear him now, so we shall know what are the limits of this debate.
(Translation):

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I hope the hon. member will take note of what I said previously. The autonomy of the provinces is not involved in this bill. This bill is purely an arrangement for the extension of a specific provision of the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Agreements Act, and I would ask the hon. member to confine himself to that subject.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say a word on behalf of the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napier-ville. As I see it, citation 418 deals in effect, as Your Honour has said, with the principle of the bill on third reading, and the principle of the bill concerns not only section 12, which is now before the house, but also concerns the other sections. It is my submission that the hon. member in dealing with the general aspects of the federal-provincial tax-sharing agreements legislation has the right to put on Hansard certain statements made by those who are members of this house.

Dominion-Provincial Relations

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I can only accept the hon. member's submission in so far as those statements are relevant to the clause of the bill. To my mind the debate on the principle of the bill on second reading is a broad debate, and there was no restriction at that time covering the whole range of federal-provincial arrangements, conferences and all those matters. But when we come to third reading the house has disposed of the principle of the bill. It has disposed of the amendments, if any, in committee, and it has settled on one clause, which is all that is before the house now. It is only in so far as it is necessary to go outside the bill to explain what the continuation of this section involves that such extraneous matters would be relevant. To my mind that is not a very wide field and I hope hon. members will accept that view and keep their attention directed to the bill as it has been accepted in committee.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I think the hon. member can do that, sir, but the point is that in dealing with the clause as it is now before the house the member is entitled to more than the ordinary latitude because of the fact that the tax-sharing agreement embraces an over-all formula. I think in so far as the formula is concerned, which formula has been adopted by the Department of Finance and the government and is being extended in this case, the member could discuss that in relation to what another member has said about the particular federal-provincial agreement.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I would be glad to hear any other hon. member, but I have not accepted what the hon. member for Laurier has said because this amendment continues a 13 per cent rate instead of a 10 per cent rate. The whole of the tax agreement of 1956 is not in issue in any way in this bill; the only thing which is in issue as I conceive it is whether or not the rate of allowance with respect to income tax shall be 13 per cent or 10 per cent. I may be wrong about that, and if I am I shall be glad to be so shown; but unless I am convinced to the contrary it seems to me that there is only this pretty narrow range for debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect, it is quite clear that the position advanced by the hon. member for Laurier is quite untenable and entirely at variance with the citation you quoted from Beauchesne. The effect of this very short bill is simply to change one figure in the main act, namely the figure 10


to the figure 13, with respect to the current fiscal year. That is what it does and that is all it does.
Mr. Speaker, there is no occasion whatever for hon. members opposite to complain that they did not have ample latitude. The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion) spoke in this house in the debate on second reading on June 3. When we last had this matter before us on May 20 I indicated that I might have something more to say at this stage about the international finance corporation. At that time I expressed some amazement at the fact we were a member of the international finance corporation when no resolution had ever been introduced into the House of Commons requesting that the House of Commons approve Canada's participation in the international finance corporation.
I have had a look at the records and I know the minister is aware of the fact that parliament never gave legislative authority for our association with this organization. However, as he intimated there was a vote passed in the year 1955. The only mention of the money involved, and of Canada's participation, occurred not in the house at all but in the estimates committee on July 5, 1955, under vote 789, "to authorize the purchase
Bretton Woods Agreements Act of 3,600 shares of stock of the international finance corporation, being Canada's subscription as a member thereof for the amount of $3,600,000, United States, notwithstanding that payment may exceed or fall short of the equivalent in Canadian dollars, estimated as of May, 1955, $3,555,000".
An hon. member of the committee asked, "Is this a usual expenditure?" Then Mr. Harris replied:
It is the first time it has appeared. The bank is not yet in existence but is expected to be by agreement of the various countries during the course of the fiscal year and we will buy our share of the stock in it.
This is a very odd way in which Canada became a member of an international organization. The minister of finance of the day announced, not to the House of Commons but to an estimates committee, that this was an unusual outlay of money, and he announced that Canada was going to become a member. Our group has reservations about our membership in this organization, because this is not a world-wide organization established to assist the peoples of other nations with the approval of the regimes or the governments of those nations. This is a means whereby an international agency is established which has the right to invest and make money in private enterprises in various areas of the world.
The organization has undertaken so far to help the Siemens company of western Germany to establish an electrical manufacturing plant in Brazil. It has assisted a branch of the Kaiser corporation to establish an automobile plant in Brazil. It has assisted numerous other large industrial organizations or concerns to invest in some of the underdeveloped areas of the world. The corporation is a money making organization. For example, the term of the loan to the Siemens company reads ". .. 6 per cent interest and option on shares". I notice that in all cases except one the organization has taken for itself options on shares.
I assume from reading the report of the minister that the corporation then markets these options. It has made no little amount of money. In the year ending June 30, 1958 it had a net income of $2,358,276. The net income the year before was $1,675,382. I can see a danger in this organization. I know the minister has made the claim that this is an affiliate of the international bank. However, I do not find that it is really an affiliate at all. I hope that some day the government is going to bring this matter before parliament in the form of a resolution or legislation, so that we may have a debate on whether or not it is expedient that Canada become a member of the international finance corporation and participate in its activities.

At that time I believe a question was raised, however, and I hope the minister will say something about it, either before we pass second reading or in committee. I refer to the announcement of President Eisenhower in August when he indicated, as did our own Prime Minister, that it seemed to be of advantage to increase the liquidity of the two funds to which we have been giving attention in this debate.
But there was a No. 3 item which some of us thought might get discussion at New Delhi at the annual meeting, namely President Eisenhower's idea about the international development bank. So that we may have it on the record, President Eisenhower indicated that he would like to see the international monetary fund contributions increased by 50 per cent. He indicated before the assembly in New Delhi that he would also like to see the capital of the world bank doubled; but he added that he felt there should be the establishment-and that is the word I read in the New York Times-of an international development bank as an affiliate of the world bank. I wonder if the minister, who attended this conference on behalf of Canada, would indicate to the house, or later to the committee, just what the difference is between President Eisenhower's conception of a new affiliate of the
[Mr. Regier.l

world bank and the one which I confess the minister did describe in the debate on May 20 known as another affiliate of the world bank, namely the international finance corporation. 1 hope the minister will comment on that.
In addition, I wonder if the minister at some stage before we complete approval of this legislation would indicate whether or not, having surveyed the scene, he concludes that the new resources of the world bank will come chiefly from new national contributions, or will they come, in the case of other countries, mostly from borrowings in the United States by the members of the world bank?
In addition to that, the last figures which I saw indicated that the world bank on concluding their last public report of June 30, 1958 indicated that in the current year they had loaned $711 million, which was stated to be three-quarters as much again as the average of the three preceding years. Perhaps there is a new figure available to the house with respect to world bank activities since this last figure which is available to me as of June 30, 1958.
Another question which I should like to ask the minister, about which 1 am not clear -I probably have not completed adequate research-is this. Has the United States congress yet done down there what is being asked of us here? Another question I would like to ask is, am I right in thinking that in dollars and cents the result not only of the increase in contributions of 50 per cent in the case of the international monetary fund and 100 per cent in the case of the world bank, but also by virtue of the extra percentage of over-all assessment which Canada has agreed to bear in the case of each one of these organizations, amounts to $100 million? That is to say, if the straight 50 per cent were used in the case of the international monetary fund and the 100 per cent increase were used in the case of the world bank, am I right in thinking that the effect would be, without the new percentage assessment that was agreed to by the minister, that we would be asked for $200 million less than is contemplated in the legislation before us?

Bretton Woods Agreements Act
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) asked about the extent of the Canadian subscriptions. Had the Canadian subscription been increased simply by 50 per cent, which is the general increase, her subscription would have become $450 million. We are asking the house to approve a subscription of $550 million, which means $100 million in excess of the 50 per cent increase.
In the case of the subscription to the international bank for reconstruction and development, Canada's subscription hitherto has been $325 million. There is no question about the legality of the proceedings taken by the Canadian parliament at that time. The former government that was in office at that time, if it had so chosen, could have asked parliament to approve a resolution in this respect. It could have done so. It did not do so. The fact that it did not do so does not render Canada's association with the international finance corporation illegal in the light of the action that parliament took. An appropriation bill passed by parliament is just as much a legislative enactment of this parliament as is any other measure that is passed by this parliament. In this case the government of the day, instead of introducing a formal resolution or a formal bill relating to Canada's joining the international finance corporation, chose to ask parliament to approve a subscription for 3,600 shares of the capital stock of the international finance corporation. It did so in the estimates and, I must say, it did so not on one occasion but on two occasions. If the hon. member thinks now that this matter went through parliament without adequate discussion, then I must recall to his mind the responsibility that he shares in that respect along with others, because he was one of those who decided on those two occasions to forego the opportunity to raise the matter for discussion.

I was asked a question about this a fortnight ago by the Leader of the Opposition. He referred to it in the discussion at the resolution stage of the present measure on May 20.
The international development association, I wish first of all to make clear, has nothing to do with the international finance corporation. The suggestion emanated from Washington and discussion on it was current in Washington about a year ago. It was known at that time as the Monroney plan. The father of it was Senator Monroney. The gist of this plan was that a new organization might be set up to provide loans in hard currency available to countries in need of loans in hard currency which would be repayable by them in soft currency. They would be permitted to repay in their own currencies.
The discussion at Washington in the spring and early summer of 1958 had proceeded to a point where it was thought that it might be the intention of the United States delegation to the meeting of the governors of the international bank and the international monetary fund at New Delhi in October to bring the matter forward as a proposal there. However, that was not done. The matter has been rather dormant in the interval. There have been indications in the press of late that the subject is to be revived. I do not think I can do better, in stating the purposes and functions of these two institutions and comparing them than to draw attention to what I said about them at the committee stage in the statement I made on May 20, at pages 3852 and 3855 of Hansard. Hon. members will find this in the second column on page 3852. I pointed out:
The international bank has, by direct loans and by arranging lor investment from other public and private sources, contributed to the long-term economic growth of many countries, particularly those in greatest need of development capital. It has also provided a pool of competent technical personnel to assist countries in working out sound development programs.
As to the international finance corporation, I said at page 3855 of Hansard, in the second paragraph:
The international finance corporation is an affiliate of the international bank for reconstruction and development with membership open only to governments which are members of the bank. Its objective is to further economic development by encouraging the growth of productive private enterprise in its member countries, particularly in the less developed areas.
Then I pointed out the means available to the international finance corporation for pursuing that purpose. There are three of them:
(1)	Investing in productive private enterprises, in association with private investors and without government guarantee of repayment, in cases where sufficient private capital is not available on reasonable terms.
(2)	Serving as a clearing house to bring together investment opportunities, private capital-both foreign and domestic-and experienced management; and
(3)	Helping to stimulate the productive investment of private capital both domestic and foreign.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution
is short and self-explanatory. Its purpose is to authorize the introduction of a bill to provide salaries for three additional judges of the superior court of Quebec, two additional judges of the trial division of the high court of Alberta and two additional judges of the supreme court of British Columbia. These additions have in every case been requested by and the necessary authority has been provided under appropriate provincial legislation. What is now necessary is for this parliament to amend the Judges Act to provide the salaries which will make it possible for us to make the appointments. (Translation):

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext:
The Minister of Justice
<Mr. Fulton) is introducing a bill providing for the salary of a greater number of judges for the superior court of the province of Quebec, the supreme court of British Columbia, and the supreme court of Alberta.
I may say that, in a general way, we are in favour of that proposed legislation since, as the minister explained, those new judges for each of those provinces, have been requested by each province concerned, which are responsible for the administration of justice.
There is no doubt that with the increase in population in Canada, the number of people amenable to courts increases, and that, sometimes, too long delays in the solution of cases become a denial of justice.
The province of Quebec is requesting the appointment of three judges to the superior court for the combined districts of Abitibi, Rouyn-Noranda and Timiskaming, of Chicoutimi and Rimouski, the appointed judges to reside in those respective districts. Those three judicial districts are under the Quebec territorial division and are quite a distance from it. There is no doubt that a judge residing in each of those districts will improve the situation of the people concerned and will be of service to the population in general.


Those appointments, which have been recommended and requested for many years by the bar association of each of those districts, were long overdue. It has never been known why those requests have been postponed until today by the Quebec governmental authorities, because autonomy is in no way concerned in that matter. The future will probably tell.
In conclusion, I hope the minister will appoint to those positions of judges men of integrity, learning and legal knowledge, who will be able to fulfil efficiently their role for the welfare of the people under their jurisdiction and of the population in general.
(Text):

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on this resolution. There have been several articles in Vancouver newspapers pointing out that the supreme court of British Columbia is roughly nine months behind in its work. If the ordinary citizen has to make use of such facilities it is certainly not justice that he should have to wait that long before his case is brought to trial.
I want to mention one other point and I suppose it is only on the resolution stage that I can do so. I refer to the fact that there is no age limit with respect to judges except those of the Supreme Court of Canada and in my view this may tend to be reflected in lower productivity as judges increase in age. I know that it is a question of the constitution but I think that something should be done so that the same age limit that applies to judges of the Supreme Court of Canada will be applied to judges in the various provincial supreme courts and courts of appeal. I can see that we will have to continue adding judges all the time if we happen to come to the point where the average age of our judges approaches 80 years. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REVISE AND CONSOLIDATE CERTAIN PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think it would be appropriate if I made a short statement on this resolution. The main purpose of the bill which will follow the resolution, if it is adopted, is to provide a separate statute regulating the pension provisions for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and to bring the pension provisions available to members of the force more closely in line with the Public Service
R.C.M.P. Act
Superannuation Act or rather with the provisions available to those having their pensions under that act.
The main provision in the present Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act providing pensions to members of the force are found in part V of that act which was introduced in 1949. But this provision covers only a limited number of members. The original provision for payment of pensions to members of the force was made in 1889. Since then five different parts have been added to the act dealing with contributory and noncontributory pensions with only occasional attempts having been made to integrate one part with the other. The result has been to create confusion and to make it almost impossible to explain correctly the various pension privileges to personnel in terms that can be understood. In addition, as a result of the conglomeration and unscientific nature of the pension provisions in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act there have arisen a number of anomalies and cases of hardship with which it is at present impossible to deal.
The purpose of the present proposed bill is to rationalize the pension provisions under one general heading and to take care, in so far as it is possible to do so by legislation, of the hardship cases.
Perhaps I might try to outline briefly for the committee the main changes that will be accomplished. As I have said, the first change is that instead of the pension provisions available being found in the same general act as that which covers the constitution and the organization of the force itself, the pension provisions will now be contained in an entirely separate statute. The new feature affecting members serving under parts II and III of the present act which have relation to pension, apart from additional opportunity being afforded them to elect to have all their service count under part V, is the provision that they may receive disability pensions for injuries sustained on duty as well as their service pensions.
At the present time members who have served under parts II and III on retirement are entitled to a retirement pension. But if later it is found that they suffer from a disability which was incurred on service they are unable to obtain benefits that are available to almost every other person in a comparable position, namely a disability pension in addition to the service pension. That anomaly is now being removed under the new bill. Hence, the provisions which will be found in the bill will take care of all cases that we know of where hardship results

R.C.M.P. Act
from disability which did not occasion retirement. It will also assist these former members who sustained disabilities and are in receipt of a small service pension.
Some of the other anomalies, or what I might describe as anomalies, which will be taken care of-I refer to anomalies causing hardship-are as follows. It is desired to permit certain members who transferred from the British Columbia provincial police to count their service with the Imperial forces, something which is not permitted at present under the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act but which they could have counted for pension purposes had they continued serving in the British Columbia police.
Another type of case is that of a member who is presently required to serve out his full term of engagement even although he may have completed his full pensionable service before the expiry of his term of engagement.
A third type of anomaly which presently exists is that a member of the force must serve ten years in the force under the present provisions before becoming eligible for a disability pension. This bill would permit a pension with only ten years' pensionable service. This is important, Mr. Chairman, in order to cover the cases of transfers to the force from other branches of the public service.
The normal provision with regard to transfers between branches of the public service is that a transferee from one branch to another can count for pension in his new branch all his service in the former branch. Under the provisions of the present Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act, if a public servant transfers into the force from any other branch of the public service his former service does not count toward his police pension. Under the new bill that service will count toward police pension and all that will be necessary is that he have ten years' pensionable service.
Another anomaly is that a member reaching the age limit for his rank with less than 20 years' service in the force cannot receive a pension at all. This provision produces particular hardship in the case of some transferees from provincial forces. It is proposed under the new legislation that ten years' service in the force will qualify a member for a service pension on reaching the retirement age.
It is necessary, in addition, to rectify certain anomalies such as the following. At the present time a member discharged for misconduct with between 20 years and 25 years of service may receive a larger pension than one retiring voluntarily with the same length

of service. This is by reason of the provisions of section 97(c) of the present act. This seems entirely unjustified and the situation is being taken care of under the new bill.
Again there is no flexibility at present with regard to pensions on retirement for misconduct. A member so retired with between ten and twenty years of service must receive either two-thirds of the normal pension or nothing. The new bill will permit such a member to receive anything from nothing up to a full pension at the discretion of the treasury board so there will not be the arbitrary division into two-thirds or nothing.
Again at present under part V a commissioned officer cannot retire voluntarily with full pension even though he may have completed 35 years of pensionable service. He must be compulsorily retired. It is intended to permit such an officer to receive a pension when he has completed 35 years of service or attained retirement age.
I said earlier that one of the main purposes was to bring the provisions for pensions available to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police more closely into line with those available to public servants under the Public Service Superannuation Act. This will be achieved in the following respects. First, it is intended in conformity with the modern approach to pensions available to public servants to provide that the police pensions in future be granted as a matter of right whereas at present under the provisions of the act they are at the discretion of the governor in council.
Second, the Public Service Superannuation Act now makes provision for deferred annuities whereas under the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act the maximum period of pensionable service in the force is 35 years. In the past if a member retired voluntarily with under 20 years of service he could receive only the return of his contributions. Our new bill will provide for either the return of contributions or a deferred annuity to commence at the age of 60 unless the member in the meantime becomes disabled, when he will be able to receive an immediate annuity, or if he should die his widow would receive a pension. This is in line with the provisions of the Public Service Superannuation Act.
Also the Public Service Superannuation Act provides for the payment of a residual amount of pension contribution to the estate of a member following the death of his widow and after his children have reached 18 years of age. This bill includes the same provisions.
I believe that covers the main features of the bill which will be introduced when the

resolution is carried. maintopic: R.C.M.P. ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE LEGISLATION RESPECTING ORGANIZATION AND DISCIPLINE

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: R.C.M.P. ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE LEGISLATION RESPECTING ORGANIZATION AND DISCIPLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker this is the second of the two proposed Royal Canadian Mounted Police bills, this one dealing with the organization and administration of the force and the disciplinary provisions under which the members will serve. It represents a substantial modernization and streamlining of the provisions governing organization and discipline.
At the outset I should like to pay tribute again to the serving members of the force from the commissioner down. I wish to make it clear that the bulk of the recommendations for this improvement and modernization came from the police themselves. 1 know that sometimes certain persons have given the impression that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police suffer from, shall I say, a certain rigidity in their approach to organizational and disciplinary problems. I think it is significant, and I want to emphasize the fact to the house and through the house to all those who are interested, that it has been my experience since assuming responsibility for the force that all members and particularly the officers, as I have said from the commissioner down, with whom 1 have come in contact have been most concerned to modernize this act and bring about certain changes which in their view would make the administration and the code of discipline of the force both more up to date and more democratic. This is not for a moment to say that there are any improper or reactionary attitudes on the part of anyone in the force; indeed, quite the contrary. I am not suggesting that under the former act there was anything undesirable. I am suggesting simply that it is a tribute to the modern and progressive outlook of the responsible officers of the force to find that they themselves are the ones who have brought forward and pressed for the modernization of their own act.
Perhaps the house would like to have a brief summary of the main provisions of this bill. With respect to the organization and administration of the personnel of the force it will be found that the bill will allow for greater flexibility and yet at the same time it will retain and in some respects improve the system by which there is an over-all control of the force by the government and responsibility of the force to the government.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
One respect, for instance, in which there will be greater flexibility and yet a proper retention of control is in the feature that the position of the civil servants who serve with the force will now be regularized. In the past, the commissioner could appoint several categories of special employees. Under the new bill there will be only one category of supernumerary special constables. All others serving with the force will be provided for on the establishment proper of the force, except only casual employees under prevailing rates, in which case treasury board approval will be necessary for the employment of such persons. Therefore, it will be seen that there is a considerable improvement and streamlining in respect of the relationship between the force and the civilian personnel employed with the force.
Particularly, I should point out to the house that the result of the bill will be that the nebulous in-between group of employees, employees who are neither civil servants nor actual members of the force, will disappear when this bill becomes operative.
With respect to another category of member, namely those who form the R.C.M. Police reserve, there is no substantial change made in this position, but a number of details have been eliminated and the general provisions for the administration of the reserve have been made more flexible.
One other point that should be noted in connection with changes in the administration of personnel is that there is provision for a new rank, the rank of chief superintendent. This rank will be interposed between the present positions or ranks of assistant commissioner and superintendent. The effect of it will be that the position of assistant commissioner will be one grade higher. This, I think, is entirely appropriate in view of the fact that in the majority of the provinces with which we have contracts for the service of the R.C.M. Police the contract divisions, as they are called, are commanded by an assistant commissioner. It is, therefore, I think, entirely appropriate that the position of assistant commissioner should be upgraded.
With respect to those features in which, as I have said, the administration has been modernized, I would point out the following. There are a number of provisions being deleted which, while some may regret that they are seeing the official indications of the end of an era, nevertheless do indicate that in the amendments in this bill we are taking account of the fact that conditions have changed. By way of historic interest and illustration of what I have said may I direct the attention of the house to section 18 (2) of the present act which provides that:

No constable shall so enter any hut, tent, wigwam or dwelling, unless accompanied by or under the order of a commissioned officer.
When I noticed this provision was being deleted I asked the commissioner about it. He explained to me that this was the sort of provision that in its wording and in its implications goes right back to the year 1874 when the force was first founded and their main duty was to deal with Indians on the western plains. In fact, their almost exclusive duty was to deal with Indians on the western plains, and in order to ensure that there might be no untoward incidents it was necessary to provide that while they had the right of search and entry, no constable should actually enter a hut, tent or wigwam unless accompanied by an officer. This, in so far as it reflected the ambit of the duties of the force of those days, has of course been entirely outmoded by the modern day conditions and the modern responsibilities under which the force operates and the responsibilities which it discharges and these provisions, for instance, are no longer necessary.
Then, again, in the new bill, one will see evidence which gives ample proof of the fact that a good part of the responsibility discharged by the force now arises under the contracts with the provincial governments and, indeed, with a number of the municipalities in all provinces except Ontario and Quebec.
I should perhaps mention that with respect to pay and allowances there is streamlining in the sense that in many cases functions formerly discharged by the governor in council are transferred to treasury board. I can reassure the house, however, that there is no loss of government control in that. If there is any difference of opinion, of course, the minister can take the matter to the full cabinet.
Another example of changes which take account of present-day responsibilities of the force is found in the provisions regarding disposition of property. This is a new provision because property comes into the possession of the force throughout the Northwest Territories, and we find that it is throughout the Northwest Territories where they discharge many functions not discharged by police in other parts of Canada. They have a multiplicity of welfare functions in connection with the Indian and Eskimo native populations, as I saw at first-hand during the course of a visit that I paid to the western areas of the district of Mackenzie immediately after Easter. There is, however, no legislation similar to that in the provinces to cover the disposition of the property coming into the

44S3
custody of the police under these circumstances, so we now have to make provision in our own act to provide for the manner in which and the circumstances under which this property will be disposed of.
I turn now to the provisions regarding discipline. Here, as I have said, the emphasis is upon making the procedures more democratic and of eliminating wide and arbitrary powers which were contained in the former act. Again I want to emphasize that the fact that these powers are eliminated and modified should not be taken and is not to be taken as an indication that there were abuses in the past; but we have felt that when we are introducing legislation to amend and to modernize the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act then, in accordance with the pattern and indeed with the desire of the senior officers of the force itself, it is better to provide what I call a democratic procedure, and particularly to provide for a review and appeal procedure in connection with those disciplinary cases.
The matter has been approached on the basis that we should create two categories of offences, minor offences and major offences. It is provided that offences against a standing order, rule or regulation which formerly involved the possibility of very severe, indeed harsh penalties for relatively minor or new offences will now be dealt with only as minor offences.
The reason I say that, Mr. Speaker, is that it was quite possible, and it always must be quite possible, to change standing orders and rules and regulations. No one, of course, is excused from an offence or from responsibility for an offence by reason of the fact that he did not know of the change. It was, however, quite possible to provide new offences in this manner and the circumstances were such that a member committing one of these new offences might find himself subject to very extreme penalities.
We have therefore provided, as I say, that all offences against standing orders, rules or regulations will be dealt with as minor offences and we have provided conversely that major offences are in general only offences against the provisions of the act itself. In providing these two categories of offences we think we have rationalized the difference in procedure and brought in a more up to date and more satisfactory code of discipline.
We have provided also for an appeal to the commissioner in the case of convictions for minor offences and, which is entirely new, we have also provided for a board of review to which appeals can be taken in the case of a conviction for a major offence.

speechtext:
With respect to custody, it is interesting to note that at the present time there is nothing in the act which prohibits the holding in custody of a member of the force charged with an offence for an indefinite period without trial. I am not saying that this was done but it was the view of the commissioner that it should not be possible to do so and that the act should be changed so as to make it impossible. We are providing in the new act safeguards and limits as to the time during which an offender can be held in custody without formal trial and disposition of his case.
With respect to the tribunals before which disciplinary cases were heard, we have removed the distinction between officers and members of the force so far as trial for minor offences is concerned and the tribunal in all cases will be the same. With respect to major offences, these must now be reported to the commissioner and the trial will be held under arrangements made by him, which removes any chance of bias in the tribunal that might result from the fact that an officer would otherwise possibly be trying one of his own men. It is now provided that the commissioner himself must arrange for the tribunal before which the trial will be held.
With respect to the laying of the charge, if a member of the force is charged with a minor offence an officer may lay the charge on his own authority but if he is accused of a major offence then the officer must report to the commissioner who will decide whether a charge should be laid and, if so, what charge.
One other important and interesting development which I think the house will approve is that for the first time we are embodying in statutory form provisions establishing the rights of an accused member of the force with respect to his trial. At the present time his rights are left to the regulation or discretion of the officer conducting the trial. We are making an attempt here and I think a successful attempt, to write into the statute the rights of the accused with respect to the holding of his trial so that he will know and have in statutory form that protection which is also available to a person tried before the civil or criminal courts.
With regard to punishment we have specified clearly that disciplinary offences must be dealt with in the disciplinary courts of the service itself, but it is also proposed that where an offence partakes of the nature of a criminal offence and is, as it were, a mixed service and criminal offence, we will confer with the attorney-general of the province in which the offence is committed so that if it should be his desire that the matter should be

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
proceeded with by way of a charge in the criminal courts of the province that desire can be taken account of.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, we have also provided in an entirely new feature of the legislation for the right of appeal by a member convicted of a disciplinary offence and have also provided for a board of review for those convicted of major offences. It is my view that this represents a substantial and important step forward in the bringing into line of the provisions of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act, in so far as organization and administration of the personnel are concerned and in so far as their code of discipline is concerned, with the conditions under which members of the force now serve and into line with the responsibilities which they must discharge, so that under the new act all members of the force and the country as a whole can feel that the best traditions of the force are being continued in the present age and carried forward into the future.

On clause 10-Supernumerary special constables.

The words in which I was interested are "without pay" in the first line.

I am not a member of the legal profession. What does that mean, only the power and authority of a peace officer?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He has the power to make arrests between one province and another and has such authority as is not held by a person who is not a peace officer.
What companies in Canada are granted the privilege of having their constables made a special part of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police force?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am informed that only two companies have this duty-not privilege. These are the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways. These are the only two companies that may employ a supernumerary special constable. In addition there is the Indian affairs branch.

On their person?

Is there a particular type of employee of the Indian affairs branch that is given this prerogative?

On clause 11-Civilian staff.
Mr. Chairman the explanatory notes indicate that this is new. I heard the minister comment on this clause this afternoon. I would like to know whether civilian

speakerposition: topic

speechtext: employees are hired by the force directly or under the Civil Service Act as it now stands?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
At the present time there are four categories of employee working in or with the force. There are the regular members, special constables, employed civilians and civil servants. There has developed an increasing tendency to intermingle the four groups and particularly the regular members, special constables and employed civilians have been intermingled in the technical and specialized personnel. This has led to a great deal of confusion and some difficulties as between these various types of employees. It is desired now to regularize the situation so that authority for the appointment of technical and specialized personnel under the Royal Canadian Mounted Police will be so regulated that such personnel may be ranked with uniformed personnel as members of the force subject to special instructions to be set out in the regulations with the same stated conditions and benefits.
The object of the legislation is to divide all personnel working with the force into two broad groups: First, enforcement personnel consisting of those employed, or likely to be employed, on duties requiring the status of a peace officer, and those include members of the force and special supernumerary constables. The second broad group is civilian personnel who will be those employed on the specialized clerical or maintenance duties and requiring qualifications other than those of peace officers. And these will be broadly speaking, as I said this afternoon, civil service members employed with the force and such prevailing rate employees as are authorized from time to time by treasury board.
I understand that. What I want to know is this. Are the civilian employees under the present act, not under the bill, hired through the civil service commission or directly by the force?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They are hired directly by the force. The civil service commission, however, sets their rates of pay.
There is no application to the civil service commission or il n'y a pas de concours?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no competition. There are not the usual civil service procedures followed, I understand. Under the new arrangement that will be done; but civilian members working with the force will be regular civil servants. With regard to prevailing rate employees, they will not be regular civil servants; they may be taken on and

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection

Is any provision being
made to protect the status of the existing members of the staff; that is to say, to integrate them into the civil service?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That, I understand, is done under the R.C.M. Police superannuation bill that we-
Will the civilian staff be covered by that legislation or by the Civil Service Act, since those people are civil servants?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The civil servants will be
covered by the Public Service Superannuation Act.

I think the minister has not got my question. There are a certain number of civilian employees now. The minister told my friend from Megantic that those employees had been hired by the force; therefore, they are not in the civil service. Now, it is usual in legislation of this sort, of which we have had many examples in the last 15 years, in the integrating of a group of employees into the civil service, to put some provision in the legislation to protect the status and indeed to integrate those people into the civil service and give them the status of civil servants. The reason I am asking is that I know how much work the reserve officers I know put into training with the R.C.M. Police. From the explanatory notes

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, that has been considered and it is not considered advisable to do so because this is a disciplinary force, and to administer the discipline and maintain the integrity of the force it is considered that the clause in its present form should remain.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw the minister's attention to subclause
2	of clause 13, which reads in part:
Every member other than an officer shall upon appointment sign articles of engagement for a term of service not exceeding five years-
This means that anyone who applies to be a constable and his application is accepted has to join for a term of five years. That is quite proper. However, the clause states that such a member may be dismissed or discharged by the commissioner at any time before the expiration of his term of engagement. It says nothing about his being discharged peremptorily or for cause. As the clause reads now, while there is a contract between the force and the member, it is only a unilateral contract. I can understand that a young man would enlist for a term of five years and feel secure, that he has an appointment for five years and that he cannot be dismissed just at the will of the commissioner; but the clause should state that he can be dismissed for cause or for some other reason, but not a peremptory dismissal. Does the minister not think that the clause needs to be changed to clear up such an unusual situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman, I do not. As I have already explained, in addition to the requirements of discipline, there are a number of special circumstances that may arise such as medical disqualification that comes immediately to mind, unsuitability not

connected with any disciplinary offence or an offence against the regulations; a variety of reasons why it is desirable to terminate the services of a member of the force.

I thoroughly agree with that.
I think the clause should state something to that effect, and say that a constable under those circumstances may be dismissed for cause.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The difficulty there is that-and that is the reason why the broad powers are left-if there is the requirement of assigning a cause it usually ends up as a blot on the man's record.
A cause such as ill health?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He would still have to have a finding of his physical condition which makes it impossible for him to continue as a member of the force. On the basis of my knowledge of the way the act is administered I am quite convinced that this is the proper way to keep the power of the commissioner to dispense with the services of members of the force, and it is very often in the member's own interest. In addition, I would point out that there is a maximum period of five years and members may purchase their discharge within that period.

I must say I have listened with greater astonishment than I have listened to anything since the present government took office to the words we have just heard from the Minister of Justice because what he has said is precisely what I used to say about not giving the reasons for not allowing persons who had no right to come into Canada to come into Canada. The minister sat over here on this side of the house day after day when my estimates were up during the time I was in office and complained about the denial of human rights because we would not give the reason why we did not let people come into Canada as immigrants. But here we are dealing with Canadians serving in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and he objects to having the words "for cause" in case it might be embarrassing or be a blot on their record.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not at all.

Perhaps the minister would
let me finish.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is so absurd it is not necessary.

There is one great difference between the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Finance. When the Minister of Finance meets an argument to which he knows of no reply he describes it as nonsense, when

speakerposition: topic

the Minister of Justice meets a similar argument he calls it absurd, but neither of these expletives is a reply to an argument.
I may say that I think there is a good deal in what the minister has said, just as I was quite convinced and am still convinced that the position I took with respect to this matter when I was minister of citizenship and immigration was a correct position, and I notice that the present government has not changed it. But it does come rather strangely from the minister to hear him say that Canadian citizens serving in the force, their livelihood depending upon their service, may be dismissed without any cause being given.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: After that tirade I would point out that there are two great differences. First, with respect to service offences we have, unlike our predecessors, provided for an appeal procedure, which is something my hon. friend refused to do when he was minister of citizenship and immigration.
That, of course-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Here we are dealing with people who have enlisted voluntarily in a force and subjected themselves to a code of service discipline which, of course, is something I do not think my hon. friend would appreciate.
May I say that the minister is wrong on both counts. The appeal procedure which I set up when I was minister is the only appeal procedure which exists in the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What that has to do with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act I do not quite understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You are getting exercised all right. I fail to see what the appeal procedure or any other procedure under the Immigration Act has to do with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act which we are discussing clause by clause at this time.

On the point of order, I did not begin to discuss the appeal board. (Text):

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Dismissal, as I have mentioned before, may be upon a number of grounds such as medical unfitness or possibly conviction of a criminal offence. Those are two which come more readily to mind. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, in order to give the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) a chance to practise his knowledge of French, I shall make a remark in my own language.
The only objection which the minister seems to have against inserting the words "dismissal for cause" in this section, seems to be that he wants to enable the commissioner to dismiss an officer without cause, for no cause whatsoever! Does the hon. minister not give too much latitude to the commissioner in this way? Let us, for instance, suppose that some day or other, the commissioner feels irritated with an officer. Then, according to this section, he might, without any reason, dismiss that officer though the latter may have signed up for five years.
As I understand it, the expression "engagement for a term of 5 years" does not mean very much, because 24 hours after a man has signed up, the commissioner may, under section 13, for no cause whatsoever, dismiss an officer who thought he was engaged for a period of 5 years.
I fail to understand why the words "for cause" could not be inserted in subsection 2 of section 13. You might mention any reason: because of illness, of politics, because of disability or incompetence; but, to my mind, the expression "for cause" would be enough to allow a commissioner to dismiss such and such an officer it would also give the opposition an opportunity to ask why such and such a person had been dismissed from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and to obtain an answer.
(Text):

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate very much indeed the opportunity I am being given to exercise my French but since I do not have sufficient command of that language to answer extemporaneously and at length perhaps my hon. friend will forgive me if I take advantage of the simultaneous translation system to answer in my own language.
(Translation):

He is getting lazy.
(Text):

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The commissioner must always give the reason for dismissal. That is the first point on which my hon. friend is incorrect. The commissioner cannot dismiss on the ground of whim or fancy without assigning a reason. The reason would be because of medical unfitness or because of conviction for this or that offence. The commissioner does not just make a ruling that the man is dismissed. As I have said, a man is entitled to request a review and on such a review there should be reasons given for his dismissal.

Furthermore, while there is no great importance attached to it, in order to keep the record straight I should point out that, as I understood the translation, my hon. friend used the word officer as though to suggest the commissioner could dismiss an officer under these circumstances. I point out that the provision of the clause makes it clear that the powers of dismissal of the commissioner under this clause are confined to members of the force.
"Member" seems to be defined to include an officer as well, according to the new definition as it has been explained. Therefore, it could apply to both.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, if my hon. friend will look at subclause 2 he will see that it says:
Unless appointed for temporary duty, every member other than an officer shall upon appointment sign articles of engagement for a term of service not exceeding five years, but any such member may be dismissed or discharged by the commissioner at any time before the expiration of his term of engagement.
The reference is to "any such member".

The Minister of Justice was very kind in making what he thought was a reply to my question, but he did not give an answer to my query. I asked him why there was no mention in subclause 2 of clause 13 of the fact there would be an appeal from the decision of the commissioner. Of course, I do not expect that there would be an appeal for health reasons, but for any other reason I do not see why the subclause should not mention that there would be an appeal. The minister did not answer my query about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is covered in the standing orders.

The minister quite properly explained that the commissioner would not dismiss anyone without cause. He cited some of the reasons why the commissioner might dismiss a constable. If that is the case, and I certainly think it is, why should the bill not say that the commissioner may dismiss a constable, either for cause in a general sense, or for certain specific reasons? A constable is bound by a contract for five years, which he signs, and I think he should be entitled to some protection if he is to be dismissed for what he may believe is an improper cause.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: May I point out to the hon. gentleman that while there is an agreement that the constable signs for a term of five years, a constable has a right to purchase his discharge. This happens with regularity.
Just what does that mean, he can purchase his discharge?

speakerposition: topic
Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand they pay a tariff, if you want to call it that, of $5 a month for the unexpired portion of their term of service. After all, a constable has received a certain amount of expensive training at the taxpayers' expense. It is therefore considered undesirable that he should be allowed to break his contract without penalty, and this is a relatively minor penalty.
The situation, therefore, is not entirely unfair to the constable. I am sure my hon. friend will appreciate, and hon. members who have asked this question will appreciate, that where you have a disciplined force such as this force is and must be on every term of engagement there is what I might call a period of experiment. It may well be found that either the member does not like the force and the conditions of service to which he has bound himself, and he is allowed to purchase his discharge, or that the officers in charge of the force find that, while this was a worthwhile experiment, unfortunately so-and-so is not going to make out well as a constable of the R. C. M. Police. Therefore, rather than have some formal hearing with disciplinary charges, in the sense my hon. friends seem to want to force on us, the commissioner, upon the report of duly qualified officers, makes a finding that this man is unlikely to become a useful member of the force so he dismisses the man from the force. There is no blot on the man's character or record. There is no trial such as would have to be held if the commissioner had to assign a cause. It has been invariably found in organizations of this nature that that is the best way to arrange a separation from the force, and particularly from a force of this kind and character.
Should an applicant be under 21 years of age, for instance, would the force require additional signatures from the parents or tutor of the applicant?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, I am informed that is not necessary. Perhaps I could supplement the answer I gave earlier with regard to appeals. I said they were covered in standing orders, and I have here paragraph 140 of the rules, regulations and orders of the R.C.M.P. It reads:
If any member of the force, other than a commissioned officer, should feel himself aggrieved by a recommendation made for his dismissal or discharge from the force, or by a conviction and punishment awarded him under the provisions of section 31 of the act, he may, within 48 hours, appeal to the commissioner in writing, stating in detail his reasons for making such appeal.
After listening to the minister one would conclude that his interpretation of the clause means that a dismissal or discharge must follow an act by

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
the commissioner himself. I call the minister's attention to the words in the second subclause, "any such member may be dismissed", but subclause 1 provides that officers of the force hold office during the pleasure of the governor in council.
Now, the commissioner obviously is not the only one who can dismiss the policeman; it must be that the governor in council has authority under this clause to provide for a dismissal. It is one thing to dismiss a police officer at the instance of the commissioner and even there, as hon. members on this side have argued, that dismissal must be with cause, but surely any action taken by the governor in council certainly ought to be on the basis of cause and on the basis of reasons given. There is nothing in this clause that would restrict the governor in council from exercising powers which he may want to exercise for one reason or another. The officer in question may have taken some action that is contrary to what the government feels, in its interests, should have been taken, or for some reason or another may want to dismiss the policeman. If there is strong ground, as I believe there is, for arguing that no dismissal by the commissioner shall take place without cause, I submit that there is a much stronger argument for insisting that whatever action may be taken by the governor in council must be taken with cause.
The minister may argue that subclause 1 does not mean what I say it means, namely that the governor in council is not given any powers under this clause to dismiss the individual concerned. However, subclause 1 can only have one meaning, that is that the governor in council has authority to dismiss. I suggest that the Minister of Justice, with his well known love for safeguarding the individual and the subject, should not in this particular instance endow the governor in council with powers which, when the minister sat on this side, he was so fond of reminding us the governor in council should not possess.

house ready for the question?

speechtext:

by reason of medical unfitness or other physical disqualifications; they are wide enough to make it impossible to discharge such persons. Therefore I must oppose the amendment.

getting up to repeat the remarks of the hon. member for Cartier. We would be very pleased to second such an amendment if it were moved at the appropriate time.

I

wonder whether the minister would reconsider the position which he took and perhaps accept the amendment as it is?

Mr. Chairman, just in
case this comes to a vote, I want to put myself on record as being against any such amendment. Any member who has any experience with a disciplinary force would not want that amendment and would not want those words in there. So I for one will vote against the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have been
asked a direct question, and I think I would have to rest upon the provisions of paragraph 140 of the standing orders, which I have already read and I will now read again. It provides that any member who feels himself aggrieved by a recommendation made for his dismissal or discharge may within forty-eight hours appeal to the commissioner in writing stating in detail the reasons for making such appeal.
I have indicated that in my view the standards of conduct of this force and the standards of discipline and of honour insisted upon by the officers in charge of the force are such that to vary this provision would strike a serious blow at the whole standing of the force. I have been at pains to explain that it is not a one-sided situation. A man who joins the force and finds he does not like the code of discipline, or any other aspect of the service, may without any grievous penalty sever himself from the service. By the same token I think it must be left available to those in charge of the administration of this force, if they find a man not suitable for the standards of physical, moral or other disciplinary conduct which they lay down to say, "Well, we regret you are not able to make the grade, and therefore without any blot on your service or any formal inquiry or charge being laid we dispense with your services."
To accept the amendment proposed by the hon. member would mean that there would have to be an inquiry, as I understand it, of a formal charge, and therefore a man whose severance from the force would be in the best interests of all concerned could not go out except upon the basis of having a blot on his record. I think that would be a very undesirable and unfortunate principle to introduce into the code of service of a force such as the R.C.M. Police.

Mr. Chairman, I think the minister has made a very sound, logical and plausible explanation, but I would like to refer to section 140 of the standing orders which he read, when he spoke about the right of an appeal. Does that also apply to all constables of the force, or to officers only?

speakerposition: topic

Who are lawyers or who have legal training. Would it not be a good thing to put in this clause:
An accused may be represented and assisted at his trial by another member who has legal training.

speechtext:
The subclause says:
An accused may be represented and assisted at his trial by another member and if the accused requests that he be so represented and assisted, his request shall be granted.

This clause shall be construed in such a way that the accused member has a choice of the member who can assist him?

I should like to know-

-if the rank of officers is considered? Is it a senior officer who hears those cases or any other designated officer?

Would this senior officer be an officer trained in legal matters, a lawyer, or a man who had some training in law?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

He would be an officer who had been thoroughly and completely trained in police matters and, as a result of that training and experience in such matters, would have acquired a good deal of legal knowledge, because my hon. friend will appreciate that a good deal of the training of R.C.M. Police members-and officers are promoted from members-indeed all R.C.M. Police officers have to know how to conduct trials or to conduct cases before the courts of the land

and therefore, in the course of that experience, such an officer would acquire a great deal of practical legal knowledge.

Subclause 3 says:

There is nothing in this subclause to prevent an accused from employing a solicitor or a lawyer.

I understand that very well; it is quite right, but does the force not appoint a defence counsel to give the accused the benefit of having the best legal service which he may desire, assuming that there is no member of the force who has legal training? speakerposition: topic
Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sure that my hon. friend, with his broad experience, must have seen many occasions when members, sergeants, staff sergeants and even corporals and the like, have appeared and conducted themselves very competently in the criminal courts of the land. So far as the penalty or punishment is concerned, would the minister be in favour of saying that the accused constable would have the right to the best legal assistance he could get?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: From among the force, yes. That is provided here.
That is just within the force.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
