On clause 35-Sentences.
When I was in the army a soldier who was tried could address the court after he was found guilty and before sentence was passed. Was a like system studied by the force in connection with this clause?

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Clause 35 provides that if the presiding officer finds the accused guilty of the offence he may sentence the accused to punishment. There is no provision for the accused to have the opportunity to address the trial officer in order to seek a lighter sentence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think this must be read with the preceding section which says that an accused may be represented and assisted at his trial by another member. I would think it would be most unusual if the presiding officer did not give the accused or his representative the right to address the court before sentence was passed. It will be noted that we have provided in subclause 6 of clause 34-again this is new because we felt it appropriate to write it into the act for the first time-that the rules of evidence at a trial shall be the same as those followed in proceedings under the Criminal Code, and while it is not specified here I think it would be normal that the presiding officer would grant that right. I would suggest that if we find that at such trials these rights are not given we would then consider the necessity of writing it into the act, but certainly it would be our view that all those procedures normally followed at criminal trials should be followed in trials under this part.

I wish to express the same fear as has been expressed by the member who spoke before the minister. Under this clause the presiding officer is prosecutor, judge and jury. The minister suggests that if they find from experience that this does not work they will consider remedying it but I think this sort of thing should be written into the legislation in order to protect the rights of the individual rather than wait for experience to prove it necessary.

On clause 36-Punishment for major offence.

Mr. Chairman, with respect to clause 36, subclause 1, I wonder whether the minister, through his advisers, could furnish us with any information at all, even approximately, as to the number, if any, of members of the force who were punished by imprisonment within the last two or three years.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am told that I am on dangerous ground in giving any estimate at all but that it would be not more than five in a year out of a force of some 5,500.

What I really wanted to know was whether there in fact had been any and that answers my question. It strikes me, with great respect, that the vesting of the power of imprisonment in officials such as presiding

officers, untrained as they would be in the law and having in mind the fact that the accused has not the benefit of any real counsel for the defence in the sense of counsel at the bar, has potential dangers inherent in it. Would the minister consider the possibility of studying the matter I have raised with a view, at some later date, to conferring back upon the courts the power that this section vests in a presiding officer?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I appreciate the feeling behind my hon. friend's remarks. I point out to him that this whole group of sections constitutes, in so far as procedure is concerned, a broadening of the powers of review and a liberalizing of the procedures which have hitherto been applicable. I point out to my hon. friend that clause 36 to which he has referred relates only to major service offences. The penalties outlined in the clause are no more severe than those which have hitherto been applicable for such offences and it is provided by a later clause, because of the very thoughts which the hon. member has expressed, that every such sentence shall now be subject to review by a board of review. This is quite new. The board of review is appointed by the minister and every such sentence, no matter what the actual nature may be, whether it be a term of imprisonment or a fine or loss of pay, is now subject to review by a board of review which is a procedure not previously available to the convicted person. We have taken a very appreciable step forward toward ensuring that there will not be an arbitrary, unjustified and harsh sentence imposed not warranted by the nature of the offence.
Can the minister tell the committee whether the procedure would be the same in the event of a capital offence within the ranks of the force?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That would be a criminal offence and without question would be tried in the criminal courts. We would not attempt to try that by a service court.
Even though the offence was committed within the ranks? There would be no fear that some evidence might be disclosed which the force would not want disclosed?

Subclause 4 of clause 37 reads as follows:
Where a person has been convicted of a service offence, the officer presiding at the trial may order that any article by means of which the offence was committed be forfeited, and any article so ordered to be forfeited may be disposed of as the commissioner directs, but any money-

Police, are anxious to see the benefit trust fund swell. If the hon. member could carry his point with the treasury board, I would be happy to see it. This clause 41 reads:

speakerposition: topic

commissioner by serving on the officer who presided at the trial or on the member's commanding officer, a written notice of appeal setting forth the grounds upon which the appeal is made.
My question is this: Here, after a member can be held, according to the act, at least 30 days before he is tried-

I was in a committee this afternoon and did not hear that. My point is that the 48 hours seems a very short time for a man to have to prepare his appeal. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think what my hon. friend does not appreciate is that there is a substantial difference between the notice of appeal and the appeal itself. This is only the notice of appeal and it sets forth the grounds upon which the appeal is made. It is not an elaborate document. It is usually a document of not more than half a page, so it is not difficult for a member to prepare a short statement setting out that he appeals and a summary of the grounds upon which he appeals. It has not been the experience to date anyway that 48 hours is an unreasonably short time within which to require that notice be served.

On that very point raised by the hon. member for Kootenay West, I may say that I had the same thing in mind that 48 hours would not be enough time to allow an accused member to give his notice of appeal. The accused member may be far away in the north or at some remote detachment or he may be sick and the mail delivery may not function properly, not because of the minister but because of the temperature.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think I can set my hon. friend's mind at rest. Trials for service offences would be held at division or subdivision headquarters. They would not be held away out at a detachment post in the wilderness, in the Arctic, so the affected member would still be at subdivision headquarters.
That is quite true, and I agree with that. If the trial is held at a subdivision office, the member may be only reprimanded, he may only lose seniority, and then

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
rejoin his old post which may be far away from headquarters. He would receive the written transcript of the evidence there, and he would still have only 48 hours. He would be far away from the subdivision office. At this point, Mr. Chairman, I should like to move an amendment. I move:
That clause 41 be amended by substituting the words "eight days" for the words "forty-eight hours" in line 4 thereof.

The
committee has heard the amendment. Is the committee ready for the question?
Amendment (Mr. Roberge) negatived: yeas, 16; nays, 51.
Shall clause 41 carry?

Would the minister accept this compromise to satisfy the difficulty that the clause creates? I can understand that a notice of appeal should be given as quickly as possible, and 48 hours appears to be reasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would be willing to accept 96 hours.

I want to go beyond that. I want to ask the minister whether he could not leave the 48 hours or 96 hours for the notice of appeal and allow 8 days for the reasons for appeal. It is a simple thing to give a notice of appeal and to say, "I desire to appeal". It is a much more difficult thing to set forth in that document the reasons for your appeal. The reasons given in the document might afterwards be held against the appellant. The appellant may want the benefit of counsel to discuss his reasons for appeal.
If the minister would, therefore, leave the time for notice of appeal at a reasonable period, 48 hours or 96 hours, and would allow the man at least 8 days to submit his grounds for appeal, this might be a reasonable compromise.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend is also guilty of confusing the notice of appeal and the argument of the appeal itself. I am sure my hon. friend has had broad experience as counsel on appeal cases. I must say that my experience has been that one of the easiest things to draw is a notice of appeal. You simply put in everything you can think of and a lot of things you know you will
not rely upon at the hearing of the appeal itself. Then, you send it off. There is not all that difficulty to which my hon. friend refers in filing a notice of appeal, stating briefly the grounds upon which the appeal is based. This is quite a different thing from preparing the case for appeal for which a great deal more time is required and will be given.

I would agree with the minister if we are dealing with a man who had the benefit of counsel all the time. If that were the case, the minister would be right. I am not confusing the notice of appeal with the grounds for appeal. Here, what is required within the 48 hours is not only giving notice but also setting up your grounds for appeal. This is a very unusual thing for a constable to be able to do as efficiently as it should be done in order to have a proper defence on the appeal.
I have noted that the minister said he would be agreeable to changing the 48 hours to 96 hours. We, on this side of the house, would accept that if the minister would have an amendment moved.

speechtext: Perhaps we could stand this clause and go on to the next one.
